aliases: how do vaccines create herd immunity

spec.concept: A disease stops spreading once each sick person infects fewer than one new person on average, which needs a share of 1 - 1/R0 to be immune.
spec.definition: Herd immunity is when enough people are immune that a disease can't keep spreading, which also protects people who aren't immune.

curve.x_label: R0: people one sick person infects when nobody is immune

prediction.prompt: In a group where nobody is immune, each sick person passes a disease to 4 others (R0 = 4). With a vaccine that always works, what share of people must be vaccinated so the disease stops spreading?

extremes.watch: a vaccine that works 80% of the time: the bar goes up

misconceptions.label: Half the people is enough
misconceptions.why_tempting: Protecting a majority sounds like it should stop an outbreak.
misconceptions.refutation: With R0 = 4 each case still causes 2 new ones when half are immune; spread only stops when each case causes under 1, at 1 - 1/4 = 75% immune.
misconceptions.source_note: Page states the 1 - 1/R0 threshold; that this mistake is common is unverified

misconceptions.label: Everyone has to be vaccinated
misconceptions.why_tempting: It feels like any unprotected person keeps the disease alive.
misconceptions.refutation: Once each sick person infects fewer than one other on average, outbreaks die out even though some people aren't immune: for R0 = 4 that's 75%, not 100%.
misconceptions.source_note: Page states the 1 - 1/R0 threshold; that this mistake is common is unverified
